concepts.name: Remainders of sums and products
concepts.description: Replace every number by its remainder before adding, subtracting or multiplying, then reduce the result once more.

concepts.name: Negative remainders
concepts.description: A number just below a multiple of the divisor can be treated as a small negative remainder: 98 is −2 on division by 100. Add the divisor at the end if the answer is negative.

concepts.name: Remainders of powers
concepts.description: The remainders of a, a², a³, … repeat. Find a power that leaves 1 (or −1), then split the large exponent around it.

concepts.name: Unit digits and cyclicity
concepts.description: The unit digit is the remainder on division by 10. Every base repeats its unit digit in a cycle of 1, 2 or 4, so the exponent only matters through its remainder on division by 4.

concepts.name: Last two digits
concepts.description: The last two digits are the remainder on division by 100. Bases ending in 1 follow a tens-digit rule; other bases are first turned into one ending in 1 (by squaring, or with 2¹⁰ ending in 24).

concepts.name: Fermat's little theorem
concepts.description: For a prime p that does not divide a, a^(p − 1) leaves remainder 1 on division by p, so exponents can be reduced by multiples of p − 1.

concepts.name: Euler's theorem
concepts.description: For a and n with no common factor, a^φ(n) leaves remainder 1 on division by n, where φ(n) counts the numbers from 1 to n that share no factor with n.

concepts.name: Wilson's theorem
concepts.description: (p − 1)! leaves remainder p − 1, that is −1, on division by a prime p. Peeling off the last factors gives (p − 2)! and (p − 3)! too.

concepts.name: Finding the number from its remainders
concepts.description: When a number leaves known remainders on division by two divisors, list the numbers that fit the larger divisor and test them against the other. Solutions repeat every LCM of the divisors.

formulas.title: Remainders of sums and products
formulas.prompt: You need the remainder of a long product or sum. What can you replace each number by?
formulas.formula:
Rem(a + b) = Rem(Rem a + Rem b)
Rem(a × b) = Rem(Rem a × Rem b)
formulas.explanation: Every multiple of the divisor disappears on division, so only the remainders survive. Reduce again whenever the working number grows past the divisor.
formulas.commonMistake: Stopping at the product of the remainders (12) without reducing it below the divisor.
formulas.applicationPrompt: Find the remainder when 46 × 73 is divided by 9.

formulas.title: Negative remainders
formulas.prompt: A number is just below a multiple of the divisor. What remainder is easiest to use?
formulas.formula:
If a = kd − s, use −s as its remainder
If the final answer is negative, add d
formulas.explanation: −s and d − s differ by exactly d, so they behave the same on division by d. Small negative numbers are far easier to multiply and raise to powers.
formulas.example:
47 × 48 ÷ 49: use −2 and −1
(−2)(−1) = 2, so the remainder is 2
formulas.commonMistake: Leaving a negative answer such as −5 instead of adding the divisor (−5 on division by 9 is 4).
formulas.applicationPrompt: Find the remainder when 58 × 59 is divided by 60.

formulas.title: Powers through a remainder of 1
formulas.prompt: How do you find the remainder of a huge power such as 2¹⁰⁰ ÷ 7?
formulas.formula:
If aᵏ leaves 1, then a^(qk + r) leaves the same remainder as aʳ
If aᵏ leaves −1, the sign alternates with q
formulas.explanation: a^(qk + r) = (aᵏ)^q × aʳ, and (aᵏ)^q leaves 1^q = 1. So only the remainder of the exponent on division by k matters.
formulas.commonMistake: Dividing the exponent by the divisor (7) instead of by the cycle length (3).
formulas.applicationPrompt: Find the remainder when 4⁵¹ is divided by 7.

formulas.title: Unit digit of any power
formulas.prompt: How do you find the unit digit of aⁿ for any base, including a product or difference of powers?
formulas.formula:
u(aⁿ) = u(aʳ), where r = n mod 4 (use r = 4 when n is a multiple of 4)
u(product) = u(product of the unit digits)
formulas.explanation: Every unit digit repeats in a cycle of length 1, 2 or 4, and all three divide 4, so reducing the exponent mod 4 works for every base. Only unit digits take part in later multiplication.
formulas.commonMistake: Using r = 0 and answering 1 when the exponent is a multiple of 4: 7⁴ ends in 1 but 8⁴ ends in 6.
formulas.applicationPrompt: What is the unit digit of 23⁶² × 18³³?

formulas.title: Last two digits for a base ending in 1
formulas.prompt: What are the last two digits of a power of a number ending in 1?
formulas.formula: (…a1)ⁿ ends in [unit digit of a × n] 1
formulas.explanation: (10a + 1)ⁿ = 1 + n × 10a + (multiples of 100), so the units digit stays 1 and the tens digit is the unit digit of a × n.
formulas.commonMistake: Multiplying the tens digit by the tens digit of the exponent instead of the whole exponent (or its unit digit).
formulas.applicationPrompt: What are the last two digits of 61⁸³?

formulas.title: Last two digits of powers of 2
formulas.prompt: What is the quick way to the last two digits of a large power of 2?
formulas.formula:
2¹⁰ = 1024 ends in 24
24 to an odd power ends in 24, to an even power in 76
formulas.explanation: 24² = 576 ends in 76, and 76 × 76 = 5776 ends in 76 again, while 76 × 24 ends in 24. So (2¹⁰)ᵏ ends in 24 for odd k and 76 for even k.
formulas.commonMistake: Applying it to an exponent that is not a multiple of 10 without handling the leftover power of 2 (2³⁵ = 2³⁰ × 2⁵: 24 × 32 = 768, so 68).
formulas.applicationPrompt: What are the last two digits of 2⁷⁰?

formulas.title: Fermat's little theorem
formulas.prompt: The divisor is a prime p that does not divide the base. Which power of the base is sure to leave 1?
formulas.formula:
a^(p − 1) leaves remainder 1 on division by p
(p prime, p does not divide a)

variables.meaning: the base, not a multiple of p

formulas.explanation: The remainders of the powers of a cycle through a set whose length always divides p − 1, so the power p − 1 always lands on 1. Reduce the exponent modulo p − 1.
formulas.commonMistake: Using it when p divides a (7¹⁰ on division by 7 leaves 0, not 1), or for a divisor that is not prime.
formulas.applicationPrompt: Find the remainder when 5²⁰²⁶ is divided by 13.

formulas.title: Euler's theorem
formulas.prompt: The divisor is not prime but shares no factor with the base. Which power is sure to leave 1?
formulas.formula:
a^φ(n) leaves remainder 1 on division by n when HCF(a, n) = 1
φ(n) = n(1 − 1/p₁)(1 − 1/p₂)… over the distinct primes of n

variables.meaning: how many of 1, 2, …, n share no factor with n

formulas.explanation: It generalises Fermat's theorem: for a prime p, φ(p) = p − 1. φ(10) = 4 is why unit digits cycle in fours.
formulas.commonMistake: Forgetting the condition: 2 and 10 share a factor, so 2⁴ does not leave 1 on division by 10 (16 leaves 6).
formulas.applicationPrompt: Find the remainder when 11¹⁰⁰ is divided by 24.

formulas.title: Wilson's theorem
formulas.prompt: What remainder does (p − 1)! leave on division by a prime p?
formulas.explanation: In (p − 1)! every factor pairs with its own reciprocal remainder except 1 and p − 1, so the product is −1. Since p − 1 is itself −1, removing it leaves (p − 2)! with remainder 1.
formulas.commonMistake: Answering 0 because "a factorial is divisible by everything": (p − 1)! contains every number below p, but not p itself.
formulas.applicationPrompt: Find the remainder when 28! is divided by 29.

formulas.title: A number from two remainders
formulas.prompt: A number leaves r₁ on division by a and r₂ on division by b. How do you find it?
formulas.formula:
List b·k + r₂ (the larger divisor) and keep the first that leaves r₁ on division by a
All solutions: N + LCM(a, b) × t
formulas.explanation: Listing for the larger divisor means fewer candidates to test. Two solutions always differ by a common multiple of a and b, so they repeat every LCM.
formulas.commonMistake: Adding the product a × b instead of the LCM when the divisors share a factor.
formulas.applicationPrompt: Find the smallest number that leaves 1 on division by 4 and 2 on division by 9.

formulas.title: Counting solutions in a range
formulas.prompt: How do you count the numbers in a range that meet two remainder conditions?
formulas.formula:
Count = ⌊(upper − first) ÷ LCM⌋ + 1
(first = the smallest solution inside the range)
formulas.explanation: Inside the range the solutions form an arithmetic progression with common difference LCM, so counting them is counting terms of an AP.
formulas.example:
Two-digit numbers leaving 1 on ÷ 3 and 2 on ÷ 5: first 22, LCM 15
⌊(99 − 22) ÷ 15⌋ + 1 = 5 + 1 = 6
formulas.commonMistake: Starting from a solution below the range (7) and counting it.
formulas.applicationPrompt: How many three-digit numbers leave 2 on division by 3 and 3 on division by 4?

levels.title: Remainders Behave Like Numbers
levels.description: Replace numbers by their remainders, use negative remainders, and watch the remainders of powers go round in a circle.

blocks.title: Swap each number for its remainder
blocks.body:
To find what 23 × 34 leaves on division by 5 you never need the product. 23 leaves 3 and 34 leaves 4; multiply those to get 12, and 12 leaves 2. So 23 × 34 leaves 2.

It works because 23 = 5 × 4 + 3 and 34 = 5 × 6 + 4: every part with a 5 in it vanishes on division by 5. Sums and differences behave the same way.

blocks.title: The remainder rule
blocks.body: Rem(a × b) = Rem(Rem a × Rem b)
blocks.caption: The same works for a + b and a − b. Reduce again whenever the working number passes the divisor.

blocks.title: Negative remainders save work
blocks.body:
29 is 1 less than 30, so on division by 30 it behaves like −1, and 31 behaves like +1. Then 29 × 31 behaves like −1, and adding 30 turns that into the true remainder 29 (29 × 31 = 899 = 30 × 29 + 29).

Numbers like 98, 99 or 26 (= 27 − 1) are much easier to handle as −2, −1 or −1.

blocks.title: Powers go round in a circle
blocks.body: Divide 3, 3², 3³, … by 7 and the remainders are 3, 2, 6, 4, 5, 1, then 3 again. Once a power leaves 1, everything repeats. 100 = 6 × 16 + 4, so 3¹⁰⁰ leaves what 3⁴ = 81 leaves: 4.
Hunt for a power that leaves 1 or −1. Spotting 2³ = 8 = 7 + 1 turns 2¹⁰⁰ ÷ 7 into (2³)³³ × 2, remainder 2, without any long division.

levels.title: Remainder Rules
levels.description: The remainder rule, negative remainders, powers, unit digits and last two digits.

levels.title: Direct Remainders
levels.description: Remainders of products and sums, negative remainders and unit digits in one step.

levels.title: Powers, Cycles and Unit Digits
levels.description: Find the cycle, reduce the exponent and handle negative bases.

levels.title: Last Two Digits
levels.description: Tens digits of powers, powers of 2 and sums of powers.

levels.title: Advanced: Fermat, Euler and Wilson
levels.description: Three theorems that tell you at once which power, or which factorial, leaves 1 or −1.

blocks.title: Fermat: the cycle always fits p − 1
blocks.body:
For a prime p that does not divide a, the remainders of a, a², a³, … always come back to 1 by the power p − 1. So the exponent can be cut down by any multiple of p − 1.

2⁶⁰ ÷ 11: 2¹⁰ leaves 1 and 60 is a multiple of 10, so the remainder is 1.

blocks.title: Fermat's little theorem
blocks.body: a^(p − 1) leaves 1 on division by p
blocks.caption: p prime and p does not divide a. The cycle can be shorter (3⁵ already leaves 1 on division by 11), but its length always divides p − 1.

blocks.title: Euler: the same idea for any divisor
blocks.body:
If the divisor n is not prime, use φ(n), the count of numbers from 1 to n that share no factor with n. Multiply n by (1 − 1/p) for each distinct prime p of n: φ(20) = 20 × 1/2 × 4/5 = 8.

φ(10) = 4 (the numbers 1, 3, 7, 9), which is exactly why unit digits repeat in fours.

blocks.title: Euler's theorem
blocks.body: a^φ(n) leaves 1 on division by n
blocks.caption: Only when a and n share no factor.

blocks.body: Check for a common factor first. 2 and 10 share the factor 2, so Euler says nothing about powers of 2 on division by 10, and indeed they end in 2, 4, 8, 6 and never in 1.

blocks.title: Wilson: factorials and primes
blocks.body:
(p − 1)! leaves p − 1, that is −1, on division by a prime p. For example 6! = 720 = 7 × 103 − 1.

Peel off factors to go further: since p − 1 is itself −1, (p − 2)! leaves 1.

levels.title: Challenge: The Three Theorems
levels.description: Huge powers on prime and composite divisors, totients and factorials near a prime.

levels.title: Advanced: Finding the Number
levels.description: Recover a number from its remainders on two divisors, and count how many such numbers lie in a range.

blocks.title: Two conditions, one number
blocks.body: A number leaves 2 when divided by 5 and 3 when divided by 7. List the numbers that suit the larger divisor: 3, 10, 17, 24, … and test each on the other: 17 ÷ 5 leaves 2. So 17 works, and so does every number 35 more: 52, 87, …

blocks.title: All the solutions
blocks.caption: Two solutions always differ by a common multiple of the divisors. If the divisors share a factor, the remainders must agree on it or there is no solution at all.

blocks.title: Counting solutions in a range
blocks.body:
How many two-digit numbers leave 1 on division by 3 and 2 on division by 5?

The smallest solution is 7; then 22, 37, 52, 67, 82, 97 step by 15. From 22 to 97 there are (97 − 22) ÷ 15 + 1 = 6 numbers.
Same remainder every time, or the same shortfall every time? Then the HCF and LCM shortcuts (LCM + r, LCM − k) are quicker. List-and-test is for remainders that follow no pattern.

levels.title: Challenge: Finding the Number
levels.description: Smallest numbers, counts in a range and a word problem from two remainders.

questions.question: What is the remainder when 47 × 53 × 61 is divided by 6?
questions.explanation: Replace each number by its remainder on division by 6: 47 → 5, 53 → 5, 61 → 1. Multiply: 5 × 5 × 1 = 25, and 25 leaves 1 on division by 6.
questions.method: Multiply the remainders, then reduce.

hints.text: You never need the full product; what does each number leave on division by 6?
The remainders are 5, 5 and 1. Multiply them and divide by 6 again.

commonMistakes: Giving 25, the product of the remainders, without reducing it.
Adding the remainders (5 + 5 + 1 = 11 → 5) instead of multiplying.

questions.question: What is the remainder when 2,341 + 5,678 + 9,107 is divided by 8?
questions.explanation: For 8, only the last three digits matter. 341 leaves 5, 678 leaves 6 and 107 leaves 3. Their sum 14 leaves 6 on division by 8.
questions.method: Add the remainders, then reduce.

hints.text: A sum leaves the same remainder as the sum of the remainders.
Divisibility by 8 depends on the last three digits, so 2,341 leaves what 341 leaves.

commonMistakes: Answering 14, the sum of the remainders, without reducing.

questions.question: What is the remainder when 99 × 98 is divided by 100?
questions.explanation: 99 is 1 less than 100 and 98 is 2 less, so their remainders can be taken as −1 and −2. (−1) × (−2) = 2, which is already between 0 and 99. Check: 99 × 98 = 9,702.
questions.method: Use the small negative remainders.

hints.text: How far is each number below 100?
Multiply −1 by −2; two negatives give a positive.

commonMistakes: Giving 98: treating the product as −2 instead of (−1)(−2) = +2.

questions.question: What is the unit digit of 1,357 × 2,468 × 919?
questions.explanation: Only the unit digits take part: 7 × 8 = 56, unit digit 6; then 6 × 9 = 54, unit digit 4.
questions.method: Multiply the unit digits and keep only the last digit each time.

hints.text: The unit digit is the remainder on division by 10; which digits matter?
Multiply 7 × 8 first and keep only its last digit.

commonMistakes: Adding the unit digits (7 + 8 + 9 = 24 → 4 here by coincidence, but wrong in general).

questions.question: Every power of 10 (10, 100, 1,000, …) leaves remainder 1 when divided by 9.
questions.explanation: 10 = 9 + 1 leaves 1, so 10ⁿ leaves 1ⁿ = 1 for every n. This is exactly why a number and its digit sum leave the same remainder on division by 9.
questions.method: Reduce the base first, then raise the remainder to the power.

hints.text: What remainder does 10 itself leave on division by 9?
A remainder of 1 raised to any power is still 1.

commonMistakes: Thinking the remainder grows with the number of zeros.

questions.question: What is the remainder when 5¹⁰⁰ is divided by 7?
questions.explanation: The remainders of 5, 5², 5³, … on division by 7 are 5, 4, 6, 2, 3, 1 and then repeat: a cycle of 6. 100 = 6 × 16 + 4, so 5¹⁰⁰ leaves what 5⁴ leaves: 625 = 7 × 89 + 2, remainder 2.
solutionSteps: 5⁶ leaves 1, so reduce 100 by multiples of 6: 100 = 96 + 4.
questions.method: Find the power that leaves 1, then use the leftover exponent.

hints.text: List the remainders of 5¹, 5², 5³ … on division by 7 until you reach 1.
The cycle has length 6. What is 100 mod 6?
100 leaves 4 on division by 6, so look at 5⁴.

commonMistakes: Reducing the exponent mod 7 (the divisor) instead of mod 6 (the cycle length), which points to 5² and gives 4.

questions.question: What is the remainder when 26⁵⁵ is divided by 9?
questions.explanation: 26 = 27 − 1, so 26 leaves −1 on division by 9. (−1)⁵⁵ = −1 because 55 is odd, and −1 + 9 = 8.
questions.method: A base one less than a multiple of the divisor gives ±1.

hints.text: Is 26 just above or just below a multiple of 9?
26 is −1 on division by 9. Is 55 odd or even?

commonMistakes: Answering 1 by forgetting that an odd power of −1 is −1.
Leaving the answer as −1.

questions.question: What is the unit digit of 7⁹⁵ − 3⁵⁸?
questions.explanation: 7⁹⁵: 95 mod 4 = 3, and 7³ = 343 ends in 3. 3⁵⁸: 58 mod 4 = 2, and 3² = 9 ends in 9. The first number is far larger, so subtracting a number ending in 9 from one ending in 3 borrows: 13 − 9 = 4.
questions.method: Find each unit digit by its cycle, then subtract with a borrow.

hints.text: Find each unit digit separately using exponent mod 4.
The unit digits are 3 and 9. Which number is bigger?
A number ending in 3 minus a number ending in 9 must borrow ten.

commonMistakes: Writing 3 − 9 = −6 and answering 6.

questions.question: What is the unit digit of 13²⁰²⁶ × 17²⁰²⁷?
questions.explanation: 13²⁰²⁶ ends like 3²⁰²⁶: 2026 mod 4 = 2, so 9. 17²⁰²⁷ ends like 7²⁰²⁷: 2027 mod 4 = 3, so 3. Then 9 × 3 = 27 ends in 7.
questions.method: Cycle of 4 for each factor, then multiply the unit digits.

hints.text: Only the unit digits 3 and 7 of the bases matter.
Reduce each exponent mod 4: 2026 → 2, 2027 → 3.

commonMistakes: Pairing 13 × 17 = 221 first and raising it to one exponent: the exponents are different.

questions.question: A number leaves remainder 4 when divided by 13. What is the quickest correct way to find the remainder when its square is divided by 13?

options.text: The square leaves the same remainder, 4
It cannot be found without the number itself

questions.explanation: Write the number as 13k + 4. Its square is 169k² + 104k + 16, and every term but 16 is a multiple of 13. So the square leaves what 16 leaves: 3.
questions.method: Square the remainder and reduce.

hints.text: Write the number as 13k + 4 and square it.
Every term with k is a multiple of 13.

commonMistakes: Answering 16, which is larger than the divisor.

questions.question: What is the remainder when 2²⁰³ is divided by 15?
questions.explanation: 2⁴ = 16 leaves 1 on division by 15. 203 = 4 × 50 + 3, so 2²⁰³ = (2⁴)⁵⁰ × 2³ leaves 1 × 8 = 8.
questions.method: Find the power that leaves 1, then use the leftover exponent.

hints.text: Which small power of 2 is one more than a multiple of 15?
2⁴ = 16. What is 203 mod 4?

commonMistakes: Reducing 203 mod 15 and computing 2⁸.

questions.question: What are the last two digits of 71⁵⁸? Enter them as a two-digit number.
questions.explanation: The base ends in 1, so the power ends in 1 and its tens digit is the unit digit of 7 × 58 = 406, which is 6. The last two digits are 61.
questions.method: Tens digit = unit digit of (tens digit of base × exponent).

hints.text: The last two digits are the remainder on division by 100.
For a base ending in 1, multiply its tens digit by the exponent: 7 × 58.

commonMistakes: Using 7 × 5 = 35 (the tens digit of the exponent) and answering 51.

questions.question: What are the last two digits of 2⁹⁰?
questions.explanation: 2¹⁰ = 1024 ends in 24, so 2⁹⁰ = (2¹⁰)⁹ ends like 24⁹. 24² ends in 76, and 76 times anything ending in 76 still ends in 76, so 24⁸ ends in 76 and 24⁹ ends like 76 × 24 = 1,824: 24.
solutionSteps: 24 to an even power ends in 76; to an odd power, in 24.
9 is odd, so the last two digits are 24.
questions.method: Group the power into blocks of 2¹⁰.

hints.text: 2¹⁰ = 1024. Write 2⁹⁰ as a power of 2¹⁰.
You need the last two digits of 24⁹. Try 24² first.

commonMistakes: Answering 76 by treating 9 as even.

questions.question: What is the remainder when 7¹⁰¹ + 9¹⁰¹ is divided by 8?
questions.explanation: On division by 8, 7 is −1 and 9 is +1. So the sum leaves (−1)¹⁰¹ + 1¹⁰¹ = −1 + 1 = 0: the sum is a multiple of 8.
questions.method: Turn each base into ±1, then add.

hints.text: How far are 7 and 9 from 8?
Use −1 for 7 and +1 for 9, then mind that 101 is odd.

commonMistakes: Treating (−1)¹⁰¹ as +1 and answering 2.

questions.question: In which step does this solution first go wrong?
questions.context:
Find the last two digits of 39⁸⁴.

Step 1: 39² = 1,521, which ends in 21.
Step 2: So 39⁸⁴ = (39²)⁴² ends like 21⁴².
Step 3: For a base ending in 1, the tens digit is 2 × 4 = 8, so the last two digits are 81.

options.text: Step 3: the tens digit uses the exponent’s tens digit (4) instead of the exponent 42
There is no error; 81 is right

questions.explanation: Steps 1 and 2 are correct. In Step 3 the tens digit must be the unit digit of 2 × 42 = 84, which is 4, so the last two digits are 41, not 81.
solutionSteps: Tens digit = unit digit of 2 × 42 = 84 → 4, so 41.
questions.method: Square to reach a base ending in 1, then apply the tens-digit rule with the full exponent.

hints.text: Check each step on its own; the first two are quick to verify.
In the rule for (…a1)ⁿ, the tens digit is the unit digit of a × n, with n the whole exponent.

commonMistakes: Multiplying by a digit of the exponent rather than by the exponent.

questions.question: What is the remainder when 3²⁰²⁶ is divided by 11?
questions.explanation: 11 is prime and does not divide 3, so 3¹⁰ leaves 1 (Fermat). 2026 = 10 × 202 + 6, so 3²⁰²⁶ leaves what 3⁶ = 729 leaves: 729 = 11 × 66 + 3, remainder 3.
questions.method: Reduce the exponent mod p − 1.

hints.text: 11 is prime. Which power of 3 is sure to leave 1?
Reduce 2026 mod 10.

commonMistakes: Reducing the exponent mod 11 instead of mod 10.

questions.question: What is the remainder when 4¹⁰⁰⁰ is divided by 13?
questions.explanation: 13 is prime, so 4¹² leaves 1. 1000 = 12 × 83 + 4, so 4¹⁰⁰⁰ leaves what 4⁴ = 256 leaves. 256 = 13 × 19 + 9, so the remainder is 9.
questions.method: Reduce the exponent mod 12.

hints.text: Fermat gives 4¹² ≡ 1 on division by 13.
What does 1000 leave on division by 12?
Work out 4⁴ = 256 and divide by 13.

commonMistakes: Using 1000 mod 13 = 12 and answering 1.

questions.question: How many whole numbers from 1 to 36 have no common factor with 36 other than 1?
questions.method: Multiply n by (1 − 1/p) for each distinct prime p.

hints.text: This count is Euler’s φ(36).
Only the distinct primes 2 and 3 matter, not their powers.

commonMistakes: Using every prime factor with its power: 36 × 1/2 × 1/2 × 2/3 × 2/3.

questions.question: What is the remainder when 7²⁰²⁶ is divided by 15?
questions.explanation: 7 and 15 share no factor, and φ(15) = 15 × 2/3 × 4/5 = 8, so 7⁸ leaves 1. 2026 = 8 × 253 + 2, so the remainder is that of 7² = 49, which is 4.
questions.method: Reduce the exponent mod φ(n).

hints.text: 15 is not prime; use Euler’s theorem with φ(15).
φ(15) = 8. What is 2026 mod 8?

commonMistakes: Using 14 (as if 15 were prime) and reducing 2026 mod 14.

questions.question: What is the remainder when 22! is divided by 23?
questions.explanation: 23 is prime, so by Wilson’s theorem (23 − 1)! = 22! leaves −1, that is 22. It is not 0: 22! contains every number up to 22 but not the prime 23.
questions.method: Wilson’s theorem for (p − 1)!.

hints.text: Is 23 prime? Does 22! contain the factor 23?
For a prime p, (p − 1)! leaves −1.

commonMistakes: Answering 0 because factorials are divisible by "most" numbers.

questions.question: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the correct option.
questions.reason: For a prime p, (p − 1)! leaves remainder p − 1 on division by p.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, R is false
A is false, R is true

questions.explanation: R is Wilson’s theorem and is true. It explains A: 22! = 22 × 21! leaves −1, and 22 is itself −1 on division by 23, so (−1) × 21! ≡ −1, giving 21! ≡ 1.
solutionSteps: So −21! ≡ −1, i.e. 21! ≡ 1. Both true, and R gives A.
questions.method: Start from (p − 1)! and peel off the last factor.

hints.text: Write 22! as 22 × 21!.
22 is −1 on division by 23.

commonMistakes: Thinking R is about 22! only and so cannot explain a statement about 21!.

questions.question: Select ALL the statements that Fermat's little theorem guarantees.
questions.explanation: Fermat needs a prime divisor p and a base that p does not divide; then a^(p − 1) leaves 1. 17, 11 and 7 are prime and do not divide 2, 4 and 5. 9 is not prime (3⁸ is in fact a multiple of 9), and 7 divides 7, so 7⁶ leaves 0.
solutionSteps: Check each: is the divisor prime, and is the exponent divisor − 1?
(c) fails: 9 is not prime. (e) fails: 7 divides 7.
questions.method: Test the two conditions of the theorem.

hints.text: Fermat’s theorem has two conditions. What are they?
The divisor must be prime and must not divide the base.

commonMistakes: Applying the theorem to 9, which is not prime.
Forgetting that a base divisible by p leaves 0.

questions.question: Find the smallest whole number that leaves remainder 3 when divided by 5 and remainder 4 when divided by 9.
questions.explanation: Numbers that leave 4 on division by 9 are 4, 13, 22, … The first one that leaves 3 on division by 5 is 13 (13 = 5 × 2 + 3).
questions.method: List for the larger divisor, test against the smaller.

hints.text: Start with the numbers that fit the divisor 9: 4, 13, 22, …
Which of these leaves 3 when divided by 5?

commonMistakes: Adding the remainders or the divisors (3 + 4 = 7, 5 + 9 = 14).

questions.question: How many three-digit numbers leave remainder 1 when divided by 4 and remainder 4 when divided by 7?
questions.explanation: Numbers leaving 4 on division by 7: 4, 11, 18, 25. 25 leaves 1 on division by 4, so the solutions are 25 + 28t. The first three-digit one is 109 (t = 3) and the last is 977 (t = 34), so t runs from 3 to 34: 32 numbers.
questions.method: First solution, then an arithmetic progression with difference LCM.

hints.text: Find the smallest number that meets both conditions first.
The solutions are 25, 53, 81, … in steps of 28.
Find the first and last of them that have three digits.

commonMistakes: Counting from t = 0 and including two-digit numbers.
Stepping by 4 × 7 correctly but miscounting the end: the last term is 977, not 1,005.

questions.question: A box of laddoos can be shared equally among 6 children with 5 left over, and among 11 children with 3 left over. The box holds fewer than 100 laddoos. How many are in the box?
questions.explanation: Numbers that leave 3 on division by 11: 3, 14, 25, 36, 47, … Testing on 6: 47 = 6 × 7 + 5 leaves 5. The next solution is 47 + 66 = 113, which is too many, so the box holds 47.
questions.method: List for the larger divisor, test against the smaller, then use the limit.

hints.text: Write down the numbers that leave 3 on division by 11.
Test each one on division by 6 until the remainder is 5.

commonMistakes: Choosing 113, the next solution, which breaks the "fewer than 100" condition.
Choosing 53, which fits 6 but leaves 9 on division by 11.

questions.question: Put the steps in order to find every number that leaves 3 on division by 8 and 5 on division by 9.

steps.text: List the numbers that leave 5 on division by 9: 5, 14, 23, 32, 41, 50, 59, …
Divide each by 8 and keep the first that leaves 3
Note that 59 is the first that works (59 = 8 × 7 + 3)
Add LCM(8, 9) = 72 repeatedly for the rest: 131, 203, …

questions.explanation: List for the larger divisor, test against the smaller, and then step by the LCM. Every solution differs from 59 by a multiple of both 8 and 9.
questions.method: List → test → first solution → step by LCM.

hints.text: You cannot step by the LCM until you have one solution.
Begin by listing numbers for the larger divisor.

commonMistakes: Stepping by 8 × 9 before checking any candidate.
